uncited: Standard Image Compression Formats refer to a family of lossy compression codecs, primarily designed for 2D texture atlases, that are adapted for volume rendering by treating volumetric data or splat attributes as dense 2D surfaces or 3D blocks.
This family solves the problem of high memory bandwidth and storage requirements for large-scale volumetric or neural rendering datasets by leveraging hardware-accelerated decompression.

All methods in this family share the mechanism of decomposing the input data into fixed-size spatial blocks (typically 4×4 texels for 2D or configurable 3D blocks), encoding each block independently using endpoint and index quantization, and providing hardware support for on-the-fly reconstruction during rendering.
**Block Partitioning:** The input data (e.g., a texture atlas representing splat attributes or a 3D volume slice) is divided into non-overlapping blocks of fixed dimensions.
For 2D formats like BC7, the standard block size is $4 \times 4$ texels.

**Endpoint and Index Encoding:** Each block is compressed by storing a small set of "endpoint" values (base colors or scalar values) and a set of "index" values (weights) that define a linear interpolation grid.
**Fixed-Rate Compression:** The compressed size is deterministic based on the block dimensions and color format (e.g., RGB vs. RGBA).
The residual range is estimated empirically to avoid clipping heavy tails, and the scale is snapped to align zero residual with an integer quantization level.
Estimate residual range as empirical [min, max] with a 2% margin over ~1.3 million samples (64 random UV positions on 20,000 surfels). 2.
Quantize uniformly with a single global (offset, scale) pair. 3.
Snap scale so residual zero coincides with an integer quantization level. 4.
Pad data to RGBA to match BC7 4x4 block layout (16 bytes per block, 1 byte per texel).
Using the full empirical range avoids this.
The foundation of this family lies in the S3 Texture Compression (S3TC) and its successors, developed by S3 Graphics in the late 1990s and early 2000s for real-time 3D graphics.
